en: A Commentary on the Meaning of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, with Preface, composed by the Śramaṇa Yuanzhao of Lingzhi Chongfu Temple at West Lake.
The ultimate proclamation of the One Vehicle ultimately points all toward the Land of Bliss; the perfect cultivation of the myriad practices is most supreme.

It is solely for the sake of the title of the fruit [of Buddhahood] that he is uniquely extolled. Indeed, it was by following his causes that he established his vows; upholding his resolve, he practiced with his own person through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, harboring the benevolence to save all beings. There was not a patch of ground the size of a mustard seed where he did not sacrifice his body. Through compassion and wisdom and the six *pāramitās*, he gathered and transformed beings without exception; the two kinds of wealth—inner and outer—were invariably granted according to requests. When the capacity arose and conditions ripened, his practice reached fulfillment and his merit was perfected; at once he realized the three bodies (*trikāya*) in their entirety, and the myriad virtues were fully manifested in the four characters.

Therefore, through the extensive praise of his wisdom, he moved the fires of hell to transform into a cool breeze; through the commendation of his virtuous friends, he beheld golden lotuses resembling the bright sun. Thus, the heavy sins of eighty billion kalpas vanished like smoke in an instant, and the distant reaches of ten trillion lands were traversed as swiftly as the shedding of feathers.

Alas! Our consciousness is clouded and our afflictions are thick; faith is meager while doubt abounds. We disparage pure practice as a provisional vehicle and deride recitation and upholding as coarse behavior. Is this not to be so addicted to this dilapidated house that we willingly endure eternal delusion, and to be so rebellious toward our compassionate parents that we deeply grieve over the total waste of this single lifetime?

One must believe that it is not by relying on other powers that the karmic afflictions can be severed without limit, nor is there any path to liberation from birth and death without encountering this gateway.
While those who hear and uphold [this teaching] are numerous, they rarely accord with the conditions of the times; and while compositions are many, few exhaust the essential meaning.

Exhausting the very tip of my hair to explain and interpret [this teaching], I dare to emulate the former masters; extending my tongue to offer praise, I vow to be one with all Buddhas. Though the Great Void may reach its limit, my humble resolve shall never end; let us respectfully exert ourselves as fellow travelers to deeply honor this Way.
In explaining this sutra, one must first summarize its essential framework through thematic categories before entering the text to interpret its meaning.

To begin with, the renowned teachings of the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One throughout his entire life, though distinguished as Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, do not transcend the fourfold scheme of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit. Through the teaching, the principle is revealed; based on the principle, practice is initiated; and through practice, the fruit is realized. These four dharmas encompass all [the Buddha's teachings] such that there is scarcely anything left unexhausted.
Regarding the initial teachings, there are generally two parts:
first, clarifying the emergence of the teaching;
second, discerning the characteristics of the teaching.
At the beginning, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha said:

'The Tathāgata, out of immeasurable great compassion, takes pity on the three realms; for this reason, he has appeared in the world to brilliantly expound the Way and its teachings, so that all sentient beings may universally obtain their share of the Dharma's benefits. He reveals the five destinies to deliver those not yet delivered, and he resolves and rectifies the path between birth-and-death and nirvana.'"
This clarifies the general intent of the supramundane teachings, which encompasses all scriptures; this is what is meant by the "universal illumination" regarding the emergence of the teaching.
Next, based on the present sutra, I shall briefly state five points:
first, the desire to cause sentient beings to know the suffering of the Sahā world and seek liberation from it; thus the sutra says:
"Sentient beings in that land have no manifold sufferings.

Second, in order to cause them to know the Buddha’s realm and give rise to joyful aspiration, the following clarifies the adornments of the primary and secondary environments, exhorting them to be born in that land.
Third, it causes the mind to be gathered and settled in the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi); therefore, the text below states:
"Upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha, one should grasp and hold his name with a single mind, without distraction," and so forth.
Fourth, it causes one to break through obstacles, escape suffering, and attain pure bliss; thus, it says below:
"When such a person passes away, their mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth," and so forth.
Fifth, it causes them to be born in that land and achieve bodhi; therefore, it says below:
"All these people shall attain non-retrogression," and so forth.
This clarifies that the primary intent of preaching this sutra is restricted to the present text, which is what is meant by the distinct narration of the arising of the teaching.
Next, we shall distinguish the characteristics of the teachings.

The teachings and contemplations of the Pure Land universally clarify the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present; this is evidenced by the passage cited below, wherein the Buddhas of the six directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, extend their broad and long tongues to exhort faith in this sutra.

Furthermore, according to the subsequent text, when good men and good women hear this sutra and uphold it, they shall all attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi without passing through gradual stages. Thus we know that all teaching gates of the Pure Lands are the methods for attaining Buddhahood through the Great Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden approach; they are certainly not partial or Hinayana, as discussed in detail elsewhere.
Second, the clarification of the principle (*li*). The principle is the essence of the teaching, which is also divided into two parts:
first, the general; second, the specific. Regarding the first:

all Mahāyāna teachings take the *vaipulya* (extensive) true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as their essence. "Vaipulya" means extensive, and "equal" means impartiality. Because the wondrous principle of true reality extends horizontally across all phenomena, it is called "extensive"; because it vertically encompasses both ordinary beings and sages, it is called "equal. Thus, one knows that all phenomena, whether horizontal or vertical, arise from conditions; they are all inconceivable and none are not true reality. This is the principle elucidated throughout the entire Mahāyāna of the One Vehicle.

Second, regarding the specific meaning: this sutra takes the inconceivable merit of the adornments of the primary and secondary bodies—attained as the fruit resulting from Amitābha’s cultivation of causes—as its expounded principle (*pratipādya-artha*). This is because, during the causal stage, he made great vows free from marks (*animitta*) and cultivated wondrous practices free from abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*), thereby attaining the holy fruit of non-attainment. Since phenomena are pointed out as being identical to principle, and marks are immediately non-marks, the body and land attained as the fruit are none other than the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, the subsequent sutra says: "As I now praise the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha. If it were not a wondrous principle, how could it be called "inconceivable"?
Third, the clarification of practice (*caryā*). Practice refers to the fundamental tenets of the teaching, which also have both general and specific aspects.

First, regarding the general clarification of the Great Practice: it does not go beyond generating the mind for supreme enlightenment and cultivating the myriad practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). These are fully contained within the various sūtras and need not be cited here in detail.
Second, regarding the specific discussion: practicing pure karma to attain rebirth in a pure land is a distinct gateway and method for transcendence.

Within the cultivation of pure karma, there are furthermore many varieties; the methods of practice shown in various sutras each differ. The *Amitābha-sūtra* (Contemplation Sūtra) teaches the three blessings and sublime contemplations; the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* (Great Sūtra) prescribes hanging silk streamers and canopies for one day and night, or observing the fast and precepts for ten days and nights; the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* (Sūtra of Great Compassion) recommends reciting the name for a single day while encouraging others to do the same; the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra* (Banzhou Sūtra) requires that if more than a day has passed, one must maintain mindfulness before them, remaining constantly without sitting or lying down for ninety days; the *Dundubhisvara-sūtra* (Drum Sound Sūtra) calls for performing prostrations and recitation at the six periods of the day and night for ten days and nights; the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha* involves reciting various divine mantras; and the *Mahābherī-hāraka-parivarta-sūtra* (Great Dharma Drum Sūtra) simply requires generating the thought that that Buddha exists.
Skillful means adapt to capacities, and the methods for practicing the Dharma are not uniform; although the gates of teaching differ, there are none that do not lead to rebirth in the Pure Land.

This present sutra specifically reveals the method of holding the Name, which is precisely the core tenet of this scripture and is essential for the present age. Therefore, it must be explained in detail and cannot be treated in a general or superficial manner.
The scriptural text may be summarized into five categories:
first, the arousal of longing and aversion—aversion toward suffering and longing for bliss;
second, the body must face west, standing upright with palms joined.
Third, fixing the period of time, whether for one day or seven days;
fourth, binding the mind to the realm of the Buddha with single-minded concentration and without distraction;

fifth, vowing not to retreat even at the moment of death, resolutely swearing to seek liberation—if even ten recitations performed under such conditions lead to rebirth, how much more so for one day or seven days?
Fourth, regarding the clarification of the fruit: the fruit is the functional application of the teaching, which also has two distinctions. First is the proximate fruit:

as the sutra says, "When this person’s life ends, their mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Because one previously recited the Buddha's name, forming the cause for karmic fruition, one abandons this defiled suffering and experiences that pure bliss; thus, one obtains the pure body of the Dharma-nature and dwells in the Pure Land of Co-residence.
Second is the distant fruit (*vipāka-phala*). As stated below:

"All beings who are born [there] shall attain non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This means that after being born in that land, they hear the Dharma and attain patience (*kṣānti*); they cultivate the path to bodhi, sever delusions, and realize the ultimate truth to become Buddhas. That is, they realize the pure *dharmakāya* and dwell in the *dharmatā-kṣetra*.
The four chapters listed above provide a brief outline; the remainder will be explained as follows, with further details deferred to other texts.
Second, regarding the commentary on the text: this sutra exists in two translations.
The first was translated by Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, which is the current edition.
II. Translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; it is currently extant in the canon.
The titles established [by various commentators] differ, as will be explained below.
Since antiquity, there have been three schools of interpretation:

The *Tongzan* (General Commentary) in one fascicle by the Tang-era Master Cien, as well as the *Shuji* (Commentary and Notes) by the present-day Masters Gushan and Hexi, both circulate in the world. What is presented here follows the respective intentions of each author; where there are occasional differences, they will be evident upon reading the text.
Next, the formal explanation consists of two parts:
first, the explanation of the title of the sutra; second, the explanation of the sutra’s text.

Regarding the first part, the original title of this sutra is “The Sutra on the Praise of the Inconceivable Merit and the Protection and Mindfulness of All Buddhas,” totaling sixteen characters. Of these, the character *jing* (sutra) serves as the general title, while the preceding fifteen characters constitute the specific title.

The first eight characters pertain to the Teaching (*śāsana*); that is, what is taught in the sutras regarding the adornment of the environment and its inhabitants, the invocation of the Name, and rebirth in the Pure Land—all of which are the inconceivable merits of Amitābha’s majestic spiritual power and the fulfillment of his vows resulting from his causal practices.

The final seven characters pertain to the Capable Recipient (*yogya*); that is, initiating practice in accordance with the Teaching, cultivating it until it becomes a definitive karmic accomplishment, receiving the secret empowerment and sustenance of the multitude of sages, and proceeding directly to Bodhi without falling back.

Master Xuanzang’s Tang dynasty translation employs the original title, *The Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Acceptance*; although the phrasing differs slightly, the meaning is essentially the same, as can be seen by comparing the texts.
In the present Qin translation, the abbreviated title is placed after the six Buddhas of the directions, immediately followed by the passage:

"You sentient beings, you should believe this," and so forth. This title was established separately by extracting the essential core according to its central tenet; it briefly possesses five intended meanings:
first, it accords with the purport of the sutra, as the scripture only demonstrates the method for holding the name; therefore, the Buddha’s name is taken to serve as the title.
Second, it is appropriate for those of lesser capacity: the name of Amitābha is what all people delight in hearing; therefore, it is used as the title because many people will believe and accept it.
Third, the principle is inherently inclusive: by merely citing the Buddha’s name, his praise, protection, and mindfulness naturally encompass all else.
Fourth, the meaning lies in its convenience and ease: the Sanskrit title contains these meanings, and through repeated hearing, one’s practice becomes mature.
Fifth, the language is concise and essential, so that later generations may uphold and recite it without prolixity.

For instance, the Tang translations adopt titles based on the original [Sanskrit], yet they have not been widely disseminated; likewise, the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Version) uses titles derived from the Chinese [florid style], yet it is rarely seen being recited or upheld. Thus we know that the Qin version deeply embodies the Sage’s intent, and for this reason it has been universally followed throughout the four seas and remains unsurpassed through a hundred generations.
The *Gantong zhuan* states that Dharma Master Kumārajīva has been translating sutras since the time of the seven Buddhas; this is indeed not false!
Now, in explaining this title, the first five characters constitute the specific (bié) designation, as they pertain specifically to the present sutra;
the final character constitutes the general (tōng) designation, as it applies to all such works.
Regarding the separate title, the first two characters designate the teaching master who speaks it; this must be Śākyamuni, though his common name is used.
The last three characters indicate the person to whom it was spoken, distinguishing him from other Buddhas; therefore, his specific name is employed.

The alternation between general and specific designations reflects the translator’s artistry; by pouring forth from my own mouth to gladden the hearts of others, and because the teaching accords with the capacities of those to be trained, it is called the "Buddha's Teaching.
*Amida* translates here as "Immeasurable. The sutra itself explains:
"The light of that Buddha is immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions without obstruction; for this reason, he is named Amida. This refers to being without limit or measure.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The lifespan of that Buddha and that of his people lasts for immeasurable and boundless asaṃkhyeya kalpas; therefore, he is named Amitābha. This refers to being beyond measure or number.

The light symbolizes the Buddha’s wisdom, and the lifespan symbolizes the Buddha’s merit; by means of this merit and wisdom, he adorns his fundamental dharmakāya. With these three virtues perfectly complete, he is established with this auspicious title; the remainder is as stated in the following text.

Regarding the general title: in Sanskrit it is called *sūtra*, which is translated here as "thread. A thread can string things together and hold them fast; this serves as a metaphor for the teaching that elucidates [the truth]. Its literary principles are continuous and interconnected, encompassing all capacities of sentient beings. Its meanings—of training in the Dharma and training in the eternal—are as explained in the standard commentaries.
Next, the explanation of the scriptural text is divided into three major sections:
first, from the beginning up to "the great assembly was present" constitutes the introductory section;
second, from "At that time the Buddha said" onwards up to "this is extremely difficult" constitutes the main body of the teaching.
From the passage "The Buddha spoke this sutra" at the end of the third section down to the final text constitutes the *Pravartanā-vibhāga* (Section on Dissemination).

Regarding the beginning and middle [of the scripture], all sutras possess both the *Śraddhā-prasāda-anuśaṃsā-nidāna* (Section of Testimony and Faith) and the *Upodghāta-nidāna* (Section of the Occasion); however, this sutra merely lists the Section of Testimony and lacks the Section of the Occasion entirely.

The preface to the *Wǎngshēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth) states: "This is a *Svayambhū-bhāṣita-sūtra* (a sutra spoken of its own accord without being questioned) among the twelve divisions of the teaching. It is like a mother caressing her infant: she does not wait for the child to request it, but simply wishes to look upon its hands and feet and nourish it with breast milk."
Now, seeking the meaning through reasoning, it can be summarized into two points:

First, to indicate that the pure lands of other directions are not the domain of the partial and limited teachings of the Two Vehicles; even if there were expedient practices [among them], they would manifest as if ignorant, yet without relying on external causes or conditions, they would speak of themselves alone to highlight their extraordinary nature. This is precisely what the Buddhas below praise Śākyamuni, saying:
"He is able to perform a most difficult and rare feat, preaching this Dharma of the world which is hard to believe."

Second, it expresses that our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses great compassion for all beings, just as a mother loves her child; pitying them for their youthful ignorance and inability to inquire, he summons them to instruct them, thereby manifesting his profound and earnest care.
Thus, the Tathāgata’s exhortation at the end states: "You all should faithfully accept my words and those spoken by all Buddhas. This is it.

Regarding the "proof of faith," this refers to Ānanda’s compilation and adherence to the teachings, wherein he established six matters as evidence to clarify that they are not false or erroneous, thereby causing sentient beings to have faith. Since the teaching does not arise unless these six conditions are complete, they are called the "six accomplishments."

The introductory sections at the beginning of various sutras have been explained in great detail; here, I shall merely provide a brief summary of the essentials, while the rest remains as it was extensively treated there. First, regarding "Thus" (*evam*):

the term "thus" is used to indicate the Dharma, specifically pointing to the dharma-gate taught in the main body of the scripture. To be "in accordance with" (*yathā*) means to accord with the principle; to be "correct" (*iti*) means to be free from error. Because one hears and retains [the teaching] through faith, it is called the "accomplishment of faith."
2. "I have heard" (*śrutaṃ mayā*) means that Ānanda himself declares he heard it directly from the Buddha and not through the transmission of another; this constitutes the perfection of hearing. 3.

"At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) refers to the beginning and end of the teaching and listening when the principal and the retinue are assembled; it excludes other times and thus constitutes the perfection of the time.
Fourth, "Buddha" refers to the Teacher Śākyamuni, who personally proclaimed this with his golden mouth; it was not spoken by anyone else, and thus it is the accomplishment of the Master.

The full term is *buddha*, which is translated as "The Awakened One. While the name "Awakened" is general, here it specifically denotes the ultimate fruit of wondrous awakening, one of the ten titles, and serves as the general title.

5. Regarding "at Śrāvastī and so forth," this indicates the locations where the sutra was spoken. Mentioning Śrāvastī refers to the sphere of his wandering and teaching; mentioning Jetavana refers to the place where he resided. Thus, the setting is established.
Śrāvastī is translated as "Renowned for Wealth," because its abundance of people and goods was far-famed throughout the various kingdoms.
It is named after Jeta, who donated the trees, and Anāthapiṇḍada, who purchased the grove, together establishing this Buddhist monastery (vihāra).

Sixth, from "together with the great bhikṣus" onwards, [the assembly] meets with the fourfold congregation of both monastics and laypeople; it is not that I alone hear this, but rather that the assembly is perfected.
There are three categories of such congregations:
first, the assembly of śrāvakas;...
2. "And all the subordinates" refers to the assembly of bodhisattvas;
3. "as well as Śakra and others" refers to the assembly of humans and devas.
Because the śrāvakas constantly attend upon the Buddha and their majestic deportment is superior, they are placed at the forefront.
The bodhisattvas manifest and conceal themselves without fixed regularity, and their forms and attire are not restricted; therefore, they are placed next [to the Buddhas].
The multitudes of humans and devas have forms and attire that are entirely different [from those of the holy ones], and thus they are listed last.
The beginning has four parts:
first, indicating the number;
second, praising their virtues by stating that they are all of the lower grade.
Third, the listing of the names of the elders;
fourth, the summary beginning with "Thus.
Regarding the first [of these two], "great bhikṣus" refers to the principal disciples, such as those listed below; the one thousand two hundred and other attendant disciples are not listed.
A *bhikṣu* (or *biqiu*; alternatively *bibiqiu*) is translated as "mendicant" (*qishi*): one who begs for food to sustain the body and begs for the Dharma to refine the mind;
it is also translated as "frightener of Māra," meaning that his resolve frightens those Māras and his virtues cause them to fear him;
it is also called "destroyer of evil," meaning that by receiving the precepts he destroys karma, and through meditative concentration and wisdom he destroys delusion.
The names of these three causes and the designations for their fruits are as follows.

"Sangha" is the full term; here it is translated as "assembly. When four or more individuals perform all *karmans* that eliminate evil and generate goodness, encompassing both the ordinary and the holy, and integrating both principle and phenomena, it is therefore called an "assembly."

When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he converted the three Kāśyapas, who together had one thousand disciples. Subsequently, he converted Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, who together had two hundred and fifty disciples. All of these were originally followers of external paths; having encountered the Buddha and attained deliverance, they constantly attended upon him out of deep gratitude for his profound kindness. Some say they are listed prominently because they were among the very first to take refuge in the Buddha, though it is not necessarily the case that they were always present at the assemblies.

Within the section praising his virtues, there are three successive instances concerning the Arhat: first, he is called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat), meaning he is capable of nourishing sentient beings, which refers to the fruit of the mendicant;
second, he is called "Slayer of Thieves," meaning he has subdued the demons and enemies, which refers to the fruit of terrifying the Māras;
third, he is called "Non-arising," meaning that fetters are exhausted and suffering has perished, which refers to the fruit of destroying evil.

That is to say, as the foremost among the assembly listed below, the great multitude of humans and devas know his virtuous deeds and recognize his appearance; therefore, he is called "one known by the multitude."

Among those listed by name, he is called "Elder" (*sthavira*) because his virtue is weighty and his years are advanced; while the term refers specifically to the first person mentioned, its meaning encompasses all ranks.

Śāriputra is translated here as "Son of the Body" (*Śarīraputra*) and also as "Son of the Eye" (*Akṣiputra*); because his mother possessed a beautiful form and her intelligence resided in her eyes, people of the time gave him this name to highlight the excellence of his mother through her son.
Furthermore, it is said that "Śā" refers to his father, Śārada, and "ri" refers to his mother, Śārikā; because both parents are clearly indicated, he is called Śāriputra, where "putra" means son.

As for Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Mahā" is translated as "Great. Since there were many with the same name, the prefix "Great" was added to distinguish him; all subsequent instances are to be understood in this manner.
Regarding Maudgalyāyana: in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, "maudga" is translated as "radish" (lài fú gēn; lài fú is read as luó pò). Paramārtha states: "Mudgara is translated as 'pea' (*hù dòu*).

Because these two items were favored by ancient seers, they named their clan after them, calling it *Nyagrodha*. This is actually the name of a tree; because his parents obtained a son through prayers to this divine tree, they named him after it."

Kāśyapa, translated here as "Great Tortoise Clan" (Mahākauravya), refers to his ancestors who practiced the Way; when a numinous tortoise bore a divine scripture in response, they adopted the clan name based on that virtue.

*Tattva* is translated as "Radiant Wave" (Prabhāsa): in ancient times, the bodily radiance of sages surged like flames, appearing like burning waves; it is also called "Outshining Light" (*Piṅgala*), so named because it can reflect other lights so that they do not appear. *Pippala* is also the name of a tree; [the name] was obtained through prayers at that tree.

Kātyāyana is translated as "Text-Adornment," also as "Hanging Shoulders" or "Beautiful Shoulders," and is also named Kola, which is translated as "Superior Thought"; all these names are derived from his clan name.

Kauṣṭhila—translated here as "Great-Knee" (Dàxī)—is also said to be so called because his kneecaps were large. He was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra; when he debated with his sister, he always prevailed. However, when she became pregnant, he could no longer defeat her. Realizing she was carrying a person of great wisdom, he departed for South India. There, he devoted himself to reciting various sūtras without leisure even to trim his nails; thus, people of the time called him the Brahmacārin "Long-Nails" (Chángzhuǎo).

Upatiṣya is also called Revata; this translates as "Constellation" (or "Star"), or sometimes "Lunar Mansion. His parents obtained him by praying to a star, and thus he was named after it. Alternatively, he is called "Provisional Conjunction" (*prajñapti-saṃghāta*). The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* refers to him as "Ever-Making-Sound. Some cite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which relates how he once stayed overnight in an empty pavilion and witnessed two ghosts disputing over a corpse. He adjudicated the matter according to reality, ruling that it belonged to the smaller ghost. The larger ghost grew enraged and tore off its hands and feet, but the smaller ghost took the corpse and reattached them. Because of these karmic afflictions, it was impossible to discern whose body it truly was; hence, he is called "Provisional Conjunction."
Furthermore, harboring doubts in his mind, he would ask everyone he met,
"Do you see my body? To which the monks replied:
"Your body was originally the remains of another and does not belong to you.
Because he attained the Way through these words, it became his name.

Cūḍapanthaka is translated as "Snake Slave"; alternatively, *cūḍa* means "by the side of the main road" and *panthaka* means "by the side of a small path," so he was named after being born by the roadside.

Nanda is here translated as "Good Joy" (Shanhuanxi) and is also rendered as "Delight" (Xinle). Originally a cowherd, he was tested by his work as a cowherd; when the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, he attained the Way with great joy. Therefore, there is a place named Gopaka Nanda, or it is said that he is the same as Upananda mentioned in the Vinaya.

Ānanda means "Joy" (Huanxi) in this language, or alternatively "Undefiled" (Wuran). When King Śuddhodana heard that the Prince had attained Buddhahood, he was filled with great joy; when King Śuklodana announced the birth of a son, the entire kingdom rejoiced, and thus it became his name.

Rāhula—translated here as "obscuration" (fùzhàng)—was the Buddha’s legitimate son. Because he was repaying past karma, he remained in the womb for six years; hence he is called "obscuration. Paramārtha states:
"Rāhu is originally called Asura, who is able to obstruct the sun and moon; one should say 'obstructing the moon. The Buddha said: 'My Dharma is like the moon.
This child obstructed me from leaving home immediately, yet life after life he was able to renounce [the world]; therefore, he is called 'obscuration.'"

"Gavāmpati" translates here as "ox-chewer" (the character for *xi* being pronounced *shī*), or alternatively as "Ox-King," or "Ox-Track. In five hundred previous lifetimes, he had served as an ox-king; because the remaining karmic retribution was not yet exhausted, he would constantly chew with a rumbling sound, leading people of the time to call him "the Ox-Chewer. It was also for this reason that he was named "Ox-Track. To avoid being ridiculed by others, he always resided in the heavens.

Pindola Bharadvāja: "Pindola" is based on his clan name; it is translated here as "Immovable," referring to that which he has realized. "Bharadvāja" is translated according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha) as "Swift"; alternatively, it refers to his faculty-nature, meaning either "sharp faculties" or "extensive speech. He belongs to one of the clans among the Brahmins.
Kālodāyin is translated here as "Black Light" (Heiguang) or "Coarse Black" (Cūhe); he was named after his physical appearance. Kapphiṇa is translated as "Lunar Mansion" (Fángxiù);
he was so named because his parents prayed to the stars and were blessed with a son.

Furthermore, when he first left home and went to see the Buddha, it rained at night and he took shelter for the night at the house of a potter. Another bhikṣu followed him there; the first bhikṣu pushed some straw over to him, and the latter sat upon the ground. The latter bhikṣu then preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the Way in a flash of realization. This latter bhikṣu was none other than the Buddha himself. Because he had shared a lodging with the Buddha under the stars, he was named after that place where he attained the Way.

Bakkula is translated here as "Excellent Appearance" (Shànróng) or "Magnificent Form" (Wěixíng). Because his physical features were upright and handsome, he was called "Excellent Appearance. At one hundred and sixty years of age, he remained free from illness and untimely death. In the past, he observed the single precept of non-killing; for ninety-one kalpas, his life was never cut short prematurely. Furthermore, because he once offered a harītakī fruit to the Sangha, his body has always been free from disease. Having received this superior retribution in the present life, he was named accordingly.

Anuruddha is also called Aniruddha, or Aniruddha; these are merely different transcriptions of the Sanskrit sound. It translates as "Free from Poverty," also as "As One Wishes," or "Inexhaustible. In the past, during a time of famine, he offered wild millet rice to a Pratyekabuddha; because his karmic retribution was fully satisfied for ninety-one kalpas, he was given this name.
In the summary, sixteen principal figures are briefly mentioned; as it would be impossible to list them all exhaustively, it says:
"such as these. The *Nanshan* states:
"Because his training followed mine, he is my younger brother; because his understanding arose from me, he is called my son.
Next, regarding the Bodhisattvas, there are three parts: first, indicating their number;
second, listing their names, beginning with Mañjuśrī.

Third, the summary as follows. Regarding the first part, although those who heard [the teaching] together were extremely numerous, the term "various" (*zhū*) is used because only four names are cited by way of abbreviation.
"Bodhisattva" is an abbreviation of a Sanskrit term; as the *Tiantai Jieshu* states:
“Mahābodhicittasattva” is translated here as “a being who has accomplished the mind of the Great Way.
Alternatively, it is said:

“Bodhisattva” is translated as “one who awakens sentient beings. “Awakening” (jue) refers to seeking the higher [enlightenment], which is wisdom; “sentient beings” (yǒngqíng) refers to transforming those below, which is compassion.

Among those listed by name, Mañjuśrī is also called Mañjughoṣa; this is translated as "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (*Miaojixiang*). "Wondrous" (*Miao*) manifests what he has realized, while "Auspiciousness" (*Jixiang*) praises his benefiting of sentient beings. Alternatively, he is called "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*), the meaning of which is the same.
He is known as a "Dharma Prince" (*dharmarājaputra*) for upholding and flourishing the lineage of the Buddhas.

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha is the Dharma King; when a Bodhisattva enters the stage of Right Dharma (*samyaktvaniyāma*) and reaches the tenth ground, they are all termed 'Dharma Princes'."
Thus one knows that this name encompasses all the subsequent positions.
Ajita is translated here as "Invincible," signifying that his compassion and wisdom are beyond the reach of those of limited or inferior capacity.
Gandhahasti is translated as "Unresting," because as long as sentient beings are inexhaustible, his cultivation of causes and realization of fruits will never come to an end.
Regarding "constant diligence," this is because sentient beings are infinite, and one never ceases for even a moment in seeking the highest [enlightenment] above while transforming those below.

To summarize: although the title "Bodhisattva" applies to both beginners and those at the final stage, as listed above, these are none other than those in deep stages who are in their last birth before Buddhahood, or perhaps provisional manifestations acting as influences; therefore, they are called "the great ones."

Third, among humans and devas, Śakra Devānām Indra—whose full name is Śakrendra—is translated here as "Capable Lord of Devas," the sovereign of the Thirty-three Heavens; the term "Dishi" (Śakra) used here combines both the Chinese and Sanskrit names. Furthermore, there are many other celestial lords such as Mahābrahmā and the Four Heavenly Kings, who cannot all be enumerated, hence they are described as "immeasurable. These are joined by the fourfold assembly of monastics and laypeople, as well as the eight classes of beings including nāgas and spirits;
therefore, it says: "The great assembly was gathered together."
The introduction is abbreviated here; the full text may be found in the *Circulation* (Prasāda) section.
Second, the *Correct Teaching* (Saddharma-bhāṣaṇa) is divided into three major parts:
from the beginning until "all gathered in one place," the text first praises the adornments of the two types of retribution, causing [the audience] to give rise to joyful aspiration.
2. From "One should not [rely] on a small or inferior [understanding]" onwards, it correctly demonstrates the method of practice by teaching the exclusive mindfulness and holding of the Name;
3. From "As I do now" onwards, it subsequently cites the praise of all Buddhas in common to exhort faith, acceptance, and upholding.
The classification of this text into three sections exhaustively elucidates the entire sutra; if one of intelligence examines it, they will realize more than half its meaning.
Within the first section, there are again two parts:

first, the general indication of the primary and secondary supports (the Buddha and his environment). The first two phrases point to the person being addressed; since he spoke as soon as the assembly had gathered, it says:

"At that time," Śāriputra—possessing great transformative power and foremost in wisdom—understood the words and grasped the meaning, deeply resonating with the Buddha’s intent; therefore, in many sutras, he was frequently commanded to engage in dialogue.
The *Maitreya’s Descent into the World Sūtra* states:
“The Great Wisdom Śāriputra is able to follow the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma; he is a great general of the Buddha-dharma.

Thus we know that while Śāriputra’s talent and eloquence surpassed his peers, when it came to this sūtra, he did not utter a single word to express doubt or inquire for clarification. From beginning to end, he was entirely addressed by the Tathāgata calling out to him; this is precisely what is meant by the aforementioned “manifesting as if ignorant,” the meaning of which is seen here.
From this point onward is the matter being addressed. The first four lines indicate the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment).

There are many types of Pure Lands as discussed elsewhere; that which is indicated here is the Pure Land of Co-residence (*sahā*). Just as with worldly nations, both the direction and the distance are fixed. Because it stands in contrast to extreme suffering, it is called "Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*), also named "Peaceful Bliss" and "Peaceful Nourishment. Although ordinary minds may doubt its distance across ten million billion lands, one can arrive in a mere instant—no more than a finger-snap or a flexing of the arm—for two reasons: first, because the pure and impure lands of the ten directions are of one mind; and second, because the movement of thought is inconceivably swift. As the *Treatise on the Ten Doubts* states:

"Provided that sentient beings bring their pure karma to fruition, the mind in meditative concentration at the moment of death is itself the mind for rebirth in the Pure Land; the very stirring of a thought is the moment of birth in the Pure Land."
For this reason, the *Contemplation Sūtra* states:
"The Pure Land of Amitābha is not far from here.
Furthermore, because the power of mental karma is inconceivable, one is reborn there in a single thought-moment; there is no need to worry about the distance and so forth.

The last three phrases indicate the primary retribution (正報); since it mentions only the transformation master, it necessarily implies his retinue. To distinguish this from the past and future, it specifies "present. From "Śāriputra" onwards, there are two parts:
first, a detailed explanation of the environment and the primary retribution, which is further divided into two.
From the beginning up to "adorned," the environment (依報) is explained; from "Śāriputra, as for your thought... onwards, the primary retribution (正報) is clarified.
This section consists of two parts:
first, a brief explanation of the names and meanings; second, from "Furthermore, Śāriputra" onwards, a detailed elucidation of its superior characteristics.
Within the first part, the initial three lines pose the inquiry, while the subsequent four lines provide the explanation.

Regarding "being free from all suffering," this is presented in contrast to the Sahā world to inspire both aspiration and revulsion. The three realms and six paths are collectively termed the fruits of suffering; within these, there are further the eight sufferings, the five sufferings, and the three sufferings.
Birth, aging, illness, death, poverty, separation from the beloved, encountering the hated, and not obtaining what one seeks constitute the eight sufferings.

The five types of unwholesome karma—killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking alcohol—are all causes of suffering that inevitably bring about the fruits of suffering; these are called the five sufferings.

The suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) are called the three sufferings. In various sutras and treatises, these names and numbers are briefly indicated; yet when one examines the world-system with discernment, everything is suffering and not a single thing is worth enjoying—not even the burning house or the prison can serve as a sufficient metaphor for it.

The realm of Amitābha’s Pure Land is exceptionally sublime, where sages and worthies assemble together to hear the Dharma and awaken to the Way. Their lifespans endure for eternal kalpas without ever regressing from Bodhi. There are other pleasures that cannot surpass this; merely being free from all sufferings is already a source of joy, let alone possessing all such superior matters—how could its bliss ever be exhausted?
Therefore, it is called "ultimate. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the joy experienced by the humans and devas in my land should not surpass that of a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

Shandao said: "If you wish to be born in that land, you must rouse your heart and discipline yourself, making the end of your life your ultimate goal. Though the physical body may undergo slight suffering for a time, at the moment the preceding thought ends and the succeeding thought arises, you will be born there. For long kalpas, you shall enjoy the bliss of the unconditioned Dharma, never again falling back into birth and death until you attain Buddhahood—how joyful this is!"

Next, in the extensive explanation of the *pariṇāmanā* (retributive) land, that which confronts the ears and eyes does not transcend sound and form. According to the conclusion of the sutra, the accomplishment of adornment consists of exactly three locations, which form three sections:

first, the railings, trees, and ponds consist solely of the adornment of wondrous forms; second, the golden ground, flowers, and music include both the adornments of form and sound; third, the warbling birds, wind, and trees consist solely of the adornment of the Dharma-sound. Therefore, the current classification differs entirely from the former; please examine the scriptural text and do not adhere to old interpretations.
Regarding the first section, the "Adornments," there are two parts:
first, from the beginning up to "fragrant and pure," which enumerates the characteristics; second, from "the relics" onwards, which provides the summary and indication.
The enumeration of the characteristics further has two parts:

Upon first arriving in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the name is revealed by citing the railings, rows of trees, and so forth. Furthermore, following the passage on Śāriputra, second, the characteristics are demonstrated by citing the ponds, pavilions, and precious lotuses.
Within the former section, the first seven phrases demonstrate the characteristics, while the final two phrases conclude the naming.

The rows of trees encircle [the pond] in seven concentric circles; each tree is eight thousand yojanas high. Because the rows stand directly opposite one another without any misalignment, the branches and leaves of these trees hang down in seven tiers above and below, all draped with nets of pearls, resembling Buddhist stupas.

The *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "Exquisite nets of true pearls completely cover the tops of the trees; upon each tree are seven layers of nets, and within the space between each net are five hundred billion palaces of exquisite flowers."
There is one row of trees and one row of railings, thus there are seven rows in total.
The "net" refers to pearl necklaces that hang further from the trees; it should be understood that these constitute all [the features].
The final two phrases merely clarify the substance of the trees and the railings.
First, gold; second, silver; third, lapis lazuli; fourth, crystal—these are the four treasures. This is the primary presentation.
According to the *Amitābha Sūtra* (*Guanjing*), the petals of the seven-jeweled lotus are fully complete;
furthermore, in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the roots, stems, branches, and leaves are interspersed with the seven treasures. Here, these are mentioned briefly; the details are found in other texts.
It is surrounded on all sides; as it is said:
"This is the case for all dwellings of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and does not mean that there are only seven layers in a single land.
The title [of this section] can be understood accordingly.
The subsequent descriptions of the various adornments are to be concluded according to this pattern.
Second, the lotus ponds and pavilions are divided into four parts;
first, the description of the pond water:
2. The stairways along the pond’s edge;
3. The pavilions atop the stairs;
4. The lotus flowers within the pond.

Regarding the ponds made of the seven treasures at the beginning and middle [of the path]: there are eight such ponds, composed of the seven treasures; the water within these ponds is also the color of the seven treasures and is called the "eight meritorious qualities":

first, clarity; second, coolness; third, sweetness; fourth, lightness and softness; fifth, lubricity; sixth, tranquility; seventh, the removal of hunger and thirst; and eighth, the nourishment of the sense faculties.
At the center of each pond is a king of wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*), from which water flows out and pours into the ponds.
Regarding the ground strewn with golden sand, the *Amitābha-sūtra* (Contemplation Sutra) states:
"The beds beneath the channels are all composed of various colored diamond sands."
"In the second [courtyard], the steps and terraces are likewise composed of the four jewels.
Third, regarding the pavilions, they are arranged with the seven treasures.
As the *Amitābha-sūtra* states:
"In these lands of various jewels, upon each world-system there are five hundred billion jeweled towers.
*Vaiḍūrya* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "not far away," because there is a mountain not far from the city of Vārāṇasī that produces this jewel.
*Vaidūrya* is also called *sphatika*; this is translated as "water-jade" (*shuiyu*) or "crystal" (*shuijing*).
Below "musāragalva," all terms are Chinese: it is like the *galva* of a chariot; *galva* refers to the rim of a chariot wheel.
Regarding the *rakta-maṇi* (red pearl), the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"It is produced by red insects; because the substance of the pearl is red.
Regarding the *musāragalva* (agate), Master Ying says:
"This jewel is red in color, like agate.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, from the ground to the heavens, the palaces, towers, pavilions, ponds, streams, flowers, and trees shall all be composed of countless various jewels and hundreds of thousands of kinds of incense, their adornment so exquisite and marvelous as to surpass that of all devas and humans," and so forth.
Fourth, the display of the lotus has five aspects:
first, its shape and dimensions; second, its manifest color; third, its radiant flames; fourth, its fragrance; and fifth, its purity—these may be seen by comparing them with the text.
According to the *Amitābha-sūtra* (Contemplation Sutra):
"In each and every pond there are sixty billion lotus flowers made of the seven treasures; each lotus flower is perfectly round and twelve yojanas in diameter."
Since it mentions "seven treasures," it does not stop at four colors.

Regarding the "twelve *yojanas*," this does not refer merely to the wheel; however, as there are large and small chariots, it is difficult to establish a fixed standard. Here, the largest does not exceed several feet, so one may take the wheel of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) as the measure.

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The golden wheel of a Wheel-Turning Sage King has a thousand spokes; its rim is adorned with various rare jewels, and its hub is made of lapis lazuli, being fifteen *li* in circumference."
According to this principle, even "less than half a yojana" refers only to the smaller [lotuses].
As for why the two sūtras differ, Cien (Kuiji) states:
"The lotuses have large and small varieties; that [sūtra] refers to the largest, while this one refers to the smallest."

Now, according to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the lotus flowers in the pond may be one yojana up to hundreds of thousands of yojanas in size; thus, we know that their dimensions differ. The descriptions in the sūtras are merely given according to what is appropriate for the occasion, and one should not necessarily use these measurements to compare the superiority or inferiority of the sūtras.

Second, regarding the conclusion and demonstration: "In this manner" refers to the various kinds of sublime characteristics mentioned above; all of these are the result of Amitābha’s bodhi-vow and practice, accomplished through cultivation over kalpas from cause to fruition.
Therefore, it is said: "Adorned with merit."
Therefore, the *Contemplation Sūtra* states:
"Such wondrous flowers are produced by the power of the vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara.
This applies to all other things as well; how could it be limited to the flowered seats alone?
The conclusion of the forty-eight vows states:
"After that Buddha had established these vows amidst the great assembly, he directed his mind single-mindedly toward adorning the wondrous land," and so forth.
The subsequent sections of the text are all explained in the same manner as this.
Second, the Ornamentation has two parts: first, the enumeration of the characteristics; [second, the detailed explanation].
Below the section on Śāriputra, there are two parts: first, the summary and indication; second, the detailed exposition.
Within the first part, there are three sections:
first, celestial music; [and so forth].
2. Golden Ground; 3. Heavenly Flowers.
First, regarding those who constantly play celestial music, according to the *Amitābha-sūtra* (Kuan-ching), there are three ways of playing music. In the "Contemplation of Water" it says:
"It is adorned with ten billion flower-pennants and immeasurable musical instruments, which are struck by eight kinds of pure winds," and so forth.
Furthermore, the description of the towers and pavilions states:

"Within those towers and pavilions, immeasurable devas perform celestial music; moreover, there are musical instruments suspended in the void that sound of themselves without being struck," and so forth.
According to the subsequent scripture, it says:
“The wind blowing through the tree-nets is like hundreds of thousands of kinds of music. Thus we know that the celestial music in that land is not of a single kind.

Second, regarding the ground being made of gold: according to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, that land consists entirely of lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya) ground, interspersed with golden cords and demarcated by boundaries of the seven treasures. What is here called “gold” refers merely to the adornment of the surface of the ground.
Third, the celestial flowers are further divided into three parts:

first, the raining of flowers during the six periods of the day, as described below; second, the offering of abundant flowers, as described below; third, returning to one's own country after the offering has been made.

To begin with, that land is constantly illuminated by light; as it lacks both sun and moon, there is no distinction between day and night. To accord with the capacities of those in this region, we speak of six periods of time. According to the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they consider the blooming of lotuses and the singing of birds to be dawn, while the closing of lotuses and the settling of birds to be night.
*Mandala* is translated here as "satisfying the mind," referring to its beauty;
it is also translated as "white flower," referring to its color.
Of these two meanings, the sentient beings of that land are collectively categorized into nine grades.
Regarding the *yike* (衣裓), Paramārtha states:
"It is a vessel used in foreign lands for holding flowers.
As soon as he was born in that land, he attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and traveled daily to other regions for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:

"At that very moment, one is able to fly and travel everywhere throughout the ten directions to attend upon and serve all Buddhas," and further: "Wandering through the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas, one hears the profound Dharma in the presence of those Buddhas," and so forth.
"Ten million billion" is used here to indicate a vast number.
Regarding the "three times," the "midday meal" refers to the period before noon. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"The palaces, clothing, food, and drink in that land are like the spontaneous objects of the sixth heaven. When one wishes to eat, bowls and vessels made of the seven jewels appear spontaneously before them, filled naturally with food of a hundred flavors. Although these foods exist, there is actually no one who eats; they merely see the colors and smell the fragrance, taking this as their sustenance, and are thus naturally satiated."
"Once the task is completed, they vanish; when the time arrives, they appear again," and so forth.
The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states:

"In the heavens of the five [desire] realms, both monastics and laypeople frequently practice *caṅkrama* (walking meditation). They come and go directly, following only a single path, like the warp threads of a loom; therefore, it is called *caṅkrama*."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"There are five benefits of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*):

first, one is capable of long journeys; second, one is able to engage in contemplation; third, one has few ailments; fourth, one digests food; and fifth, one attains long-term stability in meditative concentration."

As for "Wondrous Sound" preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, this refers to the Response-body Buddha (Nirmāṇa-kāya).
The Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are briefly enumerated by five names; hence the phrase "such as these.

Regarding the phrase "each in their own land," this refers precisely to the time when Śākyamuni was preaching this sutra: at that very moment, the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously exhorted and praised [the assembly], urging them to believe in this sutra.
If one considers the words of these Buddhas, they are not false; however, it is simply because sentient beings have heavy afflictions and hindrances that faith is difficult to attain.

The manifestation of the tongue-sign indicates truthful speech; while the tongues of all Buddhas normally reach up to the hairline, this one now appears extended and broad, its dimensions varying according to what is appropriate—how could it be limited to merely the trichiliocosm?

Next, the verses of praise are cited; one should believe these words. Following the phrase "beyond all praise," there is the title of the sutra itself. The first line refers to what was previously explained by Śākyamuni, while the latter two lines are as interpreted in the subsequent text of the sutra; the rest may be seen within the title. The final five [sections] are all explained in this same manner.

Second, among those in the south, the three—Candrasūryapradīpa, etc.—all dispel darkness; alternatively, they correspond respectively to the three bodies (*trikāya*), or they serve as singular metaphors for the virtue of wisdom.
"Fame-Radiance" (*Yaśaḥprabha*) means that his fame pervades the ten directions, just as light shines everywhere.

"Great Flame Shoulder" (*Mahārciskandha*) refers, in terms of physical marks, to the radiant flames upon both shoulders; in terms of wisdom, it signifies the simultaneous illumination of both the ultimate and conventional truths.
As for "Sumeru Lamp," the mountain lamp is a metaphor for the two bodies of Dharma and Reward.

"Immeasurable Diligence" is named after its practice; through skillful means, he delivers sentient beings without ever ceasing for a moment. Since sentient beings are immeasurable, his compassion and wisdom are likewise so.

Third, regarding the Western [Pure Land]: the first three are all termed "Immeasurable. The first refers to lifespan; the second refers to the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); and the third refers to the Dharmakāya realized therein, which is supreme and thus likened to a banner.
Great Light and Great Radiance both metaphorically represent Buddha-wisdom, which, through its own practice and its transformation of others, destroys obstacles and eliminates delusions.
As for "Precious Marks," the primary and secondary marks of the Response-Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*) are like jewels because they are precious and noble.
Pure Light is also the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya.
Question:
"If the Original Amitāyus is Amitābha himself, would it not be inappropriate for him to exhort and praise himself?"
Answer: “There are many who share that same name; he must not be the Amitābha formed from the Dharma-treasury of Sukhāvatī.
Fourth, among those in the north, Yamaṃs (Flame-Shoulder) is the same as before, except that the character for ‘great’ is absent.
"Most Victorious Sound" (*jyeṣṭhasvara*) is the same as "Exquisite Sound.

"Difficult to Pass Away" (*durdharṣa*): because the *dharmakāya* is firm and impenetrable, it cannot be destroyed; "pass away" (*dharṣa*) is pronounced *xù*, and also pronounced *jū*, meaning "to destroy.
"Born of the Sun" (*sūryaja*): just as the morning sun in the world dispels the darkness.
"Jālinīprabha" (Net-Light) refers to the fact that the dharma-gates reflect one another like the net of Indra.
Fifth, regarding the "lion" in the region below: because he is the most honored among the assembly of sages, he is compared to the king of beasts;
furthermore, just as all beasts die upon hearing the lion's single roar, this serves as a metaphor for how demons and heretics are extinguished when the Buddha preaches the Dharma.
The names "Renowned Fame" (Mingwen) and "Radiant Fame" (Mingguang) have meanings identical to those explained previously.

*Dharma* is translated as "Dharma" (*fa*); when spoken of alone as "Dharma," it refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) realized [by the Buddha], for it serves as the standard that sustains the myriad transformations.
Next, it is called a "banner" (*dhvaja*), because it rises high above all other things.
Third, as for "upholding" (dhara), it means to sustain and maintain that which is eternally abiding.
Sixth, among the names in the upper direction: "Brahma-sound" (Brahmaghoṣa) means that "Brahma" is purity; because the Dharma-sound is clear and resonant, it is heard with joy by all.
"King of Constellations" (Nakṣatrarāja): "Constellation" (nakṣatra) means excellence; the king among the constellations is the moon. As the Sūtra says:
"Among the multitude of stars, the Moon Deity is foremost.

Alternatively, it may be that the North Star dwells in the center of the heavens while all the stars revolve around it; and as the planet Mercury (Chen-xing) is the sovereign among the lunar mansions (xiu), this also serves as a metaphor for the Dharma-body transcending all phenomena.
Regarding "superior fragrance," the various virtues are like fragrances.
Surpassing all other bodhisattvas and further possessing wisdom and virtue, he is thus called "Fragrant Light" (Gandhaprabha).
As for "Flame Shoulder" (Jvālāṃsa) and "Sumeru," they are the same as previously explained and are therefore not further interpreted.

Regarding "Multicolored Jewel Flower" (Vicitraratnapuṣpa), it signifies that the causal flowers of the myriad practices adorn the resultant virtue of the Dharma-body; the meaning of the subsequent "Jewel Flower Virtue" (Ratnapuṣpaguṇa) is likewise the same.
*Sāla* is translated here as "firm and solid," for it does not wither in winter or summer; this serves as a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*, which is subject to no change.

"Seeing all meanings" refers to penetrating the profound significance of all phenomena. How can the ocean-like measure of the Buddhas' fruition-sea be exhausted? The Way is identical throughout the three periods of time, and its principle is without difference. Yet, according to the capacities of beings and in accordance with things, it is given a single name. To judge by one's own understanding, the brief explanation above is sufficient; let later scholars examine it further and refine their exposition through study.
Next, in the explanation of the title, there are three parts:

first, from the beginning up to "the Sūtra on Mindfulness," which examines the title of the preceding sūtra; since the first phrase has already been seen in the previous text, only the latter two phrases are questioned, as it is feared they may not yet be understood, and thus they are explained.
From "Śāriputra" onwards is the second part, which demonstrates the meaning, and this is further divided into two sections.
First, the section on "Hearing and Retaining" (聞持) below [the title] explains the attainment of benefits.

Regarding the initial part, "hearing the sutra and receiving it with devotion" (聞經受持), this restates the two previously mentioned adornments of retribution and formally clarifies the two major chapters on the methods of practice;

"and the names of the Buddhas" (及諸佛名) restates the previous citation of the Buddhas to encourage faith, referring to the names of the Buddhas of the six directions cited in the first sub-section of the third chapter.

Next, regarding the benefits received: "The Buddhas protect and keep one in mind until reaching Bodhi. "Protection" (hu) means to shield and guard, ensuring that one is not disturbed by Māras; "keeping in mind" (nian) means to remember and bear in mind, preventing one from falling back or losing [the path]. As the *Śixian-pin* (Chapter on Śrīmitra) states:
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions pity and remember sentient beings, just as a mother remembers her child. And as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"For example, if a fish-mother does not think of her offspring, the offspring will rot and perish," and so forth.

*Anuttara* is translated here as "Unsurpassed" (*wu-shang*); *samyak* means "Correct and Equal" (*zheng-deng*); and *sambodhi* means "Correct Enlightenment" (*zheng-jué*). These constitute the title of the Buddha’s fruition. Ordinary beings on the stage of "thinness" (*bao-di*), bound by karma and afflictions, transmigrate through the five realms for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; yet if they suddenly hear of the Pure Land and resolve to seek rebirth there, by reciting the Name for a single day, they will immediately transcend to that land. Protected and remembered by all Buddhas, they proceed directly toward Bodhi. This may be called a rare encounter difficult to meet in ten thousand kalpas, a meeting once in a thousand lifetimes. From this day forward until the end of the future, I vow to praise it wherever I am and to exhort others through various means. The bodies and lands I shall attain, and the sentient beings I shall transform, shall be no different from those of Amitābha. This heart of mine is boundless; only the Buddhas can bear witness to it.

Therefore, the third [section] below encourages faith; "those who believe my words" refers to believing the teaching. If you do not believe me, would the Buddhas of the ten directions ever speak falsely?
Next, regarding the causes and effects of the three periods of time: the first section provides the direct exposition;
the second section, beginning with "Therefore," provides the conclusion and exhortation.

Within the first section, "has already" refers to the past, "now" refers to the present, and "shall" refers to the future. Aspiring is the cause, and being born [in the Pure Land] is the effect. The three causes and three effects can be understood through their respective correspondences. To manifest the Pure Land, one only fears a lack of aspiration; if there is aspiration, birth [there] is certain and there will surely be no failure.
The *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*) states:
"Once born in that land, all attain non-arising; not a single person shall fall back into the triple world to be bound by the karma of birth and death," and so forth.

Next, regarding the concluding exhortation: if there are those with faith, they are distinguished from those without; it is left to those who do not make vows to willingly sink into mire and fire—of whom is this the fault?
Third, within the section on the mutual praise of the Buddhas, there are two parts:
first, my praise of the Buddhas; second, the Buddhas' praise of me.

The first section, beginning with "As I am now," refers back to the previous chapter on the exhortation to have faith through the six directions. Within this second part, there are two further divisions:
first, the presentation of their words of praise;
and second, from "You should know" onwards, the demonstration of their sincerity.

At the beginning, Śākyamuni is translated as "Capable Benevolence" (Néng-rén), which signifies the bestowal of great compassion through responsive manifestation; Muni is translated as "Silent Stillness" (Jímò), which signifies wondrous wisdom that merges with the ultimate truth. When these are combined to form "Buddha," the three bodies (trikāya) are complete. Because others cannot achieve this, it is extremely difficult; because the world has not yet seen such a being, it is rare.

Regarding the following two difficulties: the first is the difficulty of practicing and attaining Buddhahood in this degenerate age; the second is the difficulty of preaching this Dharma-gate for the sake of all sentient beings.
First, regarding *Saha*, it is also called *Sosha*; this translates as "Endurance. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:

"Because these sentient beings endure the three poisons and all afflictions. According to the *Buddhakṣetra Sūtra*, there are two meanings: [the endurance of suffering and the endurance of the Dharma].
The first meaning is as explained above;

second, it refers to those who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle and have accomplished patience (*kṣānti*), protecting sentient beings and skillfully disciplining themselves. Even if others inflict harm upon them, they are able to endure it all and never become negligent; therefore, it is called "Endurance" (*Kṣānti*).
The five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) are also called the five dregs; they are further termed "evil" because they enable one to fully commit the ten unwholesome karmas.

*Kalpa* (劫), in Sanskrit, is translated here as "time-period. The latter four turbidities aggregate during this period; specifically, the kalpa-turbidity begins when the human lifespan decreases from twenty thousand years.

As for "views" (*dṛṣṭi*), these are the five sharp fetters: the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
The "afflictions" (kleśa) refer to the five dull proclivities: greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt.
"Sentient beings" (sattva) refers to those who grasp at the aggregates (skandha) as a person, designated by the provisional name "sentient being.
"Life" (jīvita) refers to the momentary arising and ceasing that hastens the years and shortens the lifespan.

Regarding the second objection: the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha makes no distinction between the foolish and the wise, nor does it select between the noble and the lowly; it takes no account of the duration of practice, nor does it choose between the virtuous and the wicked. It requires only a resolute vow and fierce faith, such that even at the moment of death, through ten recitations amidst evil omens, one attains rebirth in the Pure Land. This is a method for ordinary, ignorant beings bound by all fetters—even those of the lowest sort, such as butchers and wine-sellers—to transcend their state and achieve Buddhahood in a single instant. Truly, this can be called something most difficult for the entire world to believe.
Second, regarding the "Manifestation of Reality" (*dharmatā-deśanā*): following the two preceding challenges, it is shown that what is praised by all Buddhas is not in vain;

the intent is to cause sentient beings to hear it and receive it with faith. Third, the "Circulation Section" (*parīndanā*): as the formal teaching has concluded, the assembly joyfully accepts and maintains it, transmitting it from one to another until it pervades the four seas and endures for ten thousand generations; thus, the dispersal of the assembly serves as the occasion for its circulation.
All worlds are subsumed within four categories, yet three destinies are specifically cited here to resolve the introductory text.
Asuras are translated here as "Non-Gods" (fei-tian); they enjoy pleasures like the gods but harbor deceit like ghosts, and thus their name is derived from their conduct.

Joy is the gateway for transcending existence; through faith and acceptance, one then recollects, upholds, and practices the Dharma. Having attained the Dharma within one's breast, one looks up to its grace and bears its virtue, offering sincere homage and vowing that it shall be widely disseminated.
